paras: The killing of Pap Ryland and threatened lynching of C. A. Babcock took place on the Sweetwater in western Colorado in late August 1888, when Babcock shot the aged rancher Ryland and Ryland's neighbors talked of lynching him. Babcock escaped on horseback to Dotsero, took a train to Glenwood Springs and surrendered to a deputy sheriff, and by October he was on trial at Glenwood. Papers treated the case as the death of a pioneer 'character' and as a narrow escape from a mob.

Ryland owned a ranch on the Sweetwater that had long been a landmark and stopping place for travelers and hunters. The Omaha Bee described him as 'the last remnant of the white men' who had settled on Ute hunting grounds, while the Evening World called his ranch the first located in that section and traced his career through early mining camps. Little was known of Babcock beyond his being a large man about 35 years old.

According to a Denver dispatch, Babcock shot Ryland early on Monday morning, August 27, while the two men were alone at the ranch. When the ranchers on the Sweetwater learned of the shooting they gathered and 'began to talk freely of lynching Babcock'. While they deliberated, a friend of Babcock put him on a horse, and he rode sixteen miles to Dotsero in time to catch the morning train for Glenwood Springs. A Salida dispatch put it more briefly, saying he caught the train 'in the nick of time to save being lynched by Ryland's neighbors'.

At Glenwood Springs, Babcock gave himself up to Deputy Sheriff Little and said he had shot Ryland in self-defense. The dispatches described his story as 'very conflicting' or 'confused and distorted'. Ryland died of the wound, on the evening of August 27 by the Salida account or a day later by the Denver one.

In mid-October the Meeker Herald reported that Babcock's trial was in progress at Glenwood. The paper, which named him Herman C. Babcock and the dead man J. M. Riland, said additional facts learned at the county seat made the case 'look very bad for Babcock' and called the killing the most 'wanton and unprovoked' murder in Garfield County's history. No report of the verdict appears in the coverage.

The story reached distant papers through two specials: a Salida telegram to the Omaha Bee headed 'A COLORADO CHARACTER' and a Denver dispatch to the New York Evening World headed 'The Murderer Mounts a Horse and Escapes Being Lynched'. Both called Babcock a murderer and doubted his self-defense claim, though the Bee allowed that Ryland 'was of an irascible temperament'. The Evening World cast the shooting as one of the 'mysterious tragedies' of the isolated Colorado mountains, and neither paper criticized the ranchers' lynching talk.

The Connecticut Western News ran a one-line brief placing the shooting 'near Denver', and the Phillipsburg Herald in Kansas reprinted the Salida dispatch almost word for word in late September. Closer to home, the Meeker Herald called Ryland 'law-abiding and peaceably disposed' and, while hoping for justice at trial, wrote that 'Hanging is not any too good for such a wretch'. No paper stated the race of anyone involved.

reader.title: Killing of Pap Ryland and threatened lynching of C. A. Babcock
bases: After Babcock shot Ryland, Ryland's neighbors on the Sweetwater gathered and talked of lynching him, but he escaped by train and surrendered to a deputy sheriff, so the lynching was only threatened (A1, A2).

No one was killed by the ranchers: Babcock escaped before they acted and surrendered to Deputy Sheriff Little (A1, A2); the gathering of 'ranchers' had no lawful authority and aimed to punish the killing of Ryland, but its size is not given.

Separate Salida (A1) and Denver (A2) dispatches, worded differently, agree on the shooting, the lynching threat, the escape via Dotsero and the surrender at Glenwood Springs, and the local Meeker Herald (A5) confirms the killing and a later trial.

accounts.label: Salida dispatch
accounts.gist: Babcock rode to Dotsero and caught the train in time to avoid being lynched by Ryland's neighbors; his self-defense story was conflicting and the writer doubted Ryland had attacked him.

accounts.label: Denver dispatch
accounts.gist: The ranchers gathered and talked of lynching; a friend got Babcock onto a horse while they deliberated; the two men had been alone and Babcock's account was 'confused and distorted'.

accounts.label: Babcock's claim
accounts.gist: Babcock said he shot Ryland in self-defense.

accounts.label: Local editorial (Meeker Herald)
accounts.gist: Additional facts learned at the county seat made the case 'look very bad for Babcock'; the murder was unprovoked and his trial was under way.

framing.detail: The Bee headlined 'A COLORADO CHARACTER' and presented the near-lynching as a narrow escape, while doubting Babcock's self-defense claim.
The Evening World headlined 'PAP RILAND SHOT. The Murderer Mounts a Horse and Escapes Being Lynched', calling Babcock 'The Murderer' and the case one of Colorado's 'mysterious tragedies'.
Small papers ran a one-line brief or a reprint of the Salida dispatch.
The Meeker Herald urged legal punishment ('we hope justice will be meted out to him') while saying 'Hanging is not any too good for such a wretch'.

record_check.dossier: Only C. A. Babcock (Herman C. Babcock in A5) was threatened; no 'G. A. Babcock' appears. Pap Ryland was the man killed, by Babcock, not by the mob.
The shooting and the lynching talk were at Ryland's ranch on the Sweetwater; Dotsero was the rail stop 16 miles away where Babcock caught the train.
No wire report names a county; the Meeker Herald places the murder in Garfield County.
Murder of Pap Ryland (Babcock claimed self-defense).
Ryland's neighbors, the ranchers on the Sweetwater.
Punishment for the killing of Ryland.
C. A. Babcock; the escape was aided by a friend (A2), and Babcock was later tried at Glenwood (A5).
At least four papers (Omaha Bee, Evening World, Connecticut Western News, Phillipsburg Herald) plus a local follow-up in the Meeker Herald.
